stimuli.title: The Squirrel and the Snail
stimuli.text:
In the fall, Squirrel and Snail both gathered acorns for the winter. Squirrel stuffed his cheeks with five acorns at a time and raced up the tree. On the way, he dropped three of them every trip.

Snail carried one acorn at a time. She moved slowly, but she never dropped a single one.

When the snow came, Squirrel looked at his small pile. Then he looked at Snail's tall, neat pile. "How did you get so many?" he asked.

"I only carried what I could hold," said Snail.

stimuli.title: The Amazing Octopus
stimuli.text:
The octopus may be one of the most unusual animals in the ocean. It has eight arms, and each arm is covered with suction cups that help it grab food. An octopus has three hearts and blue blood. It has no bones at all, so it can squeeze through very small cracks.

An octopus can also change the color of its skin in less than a second. This helps it hide from enemies. If hiding does not work, it can squirt a cloud of dark ink and swim away.

stimuli.title: Rain on the Roof
stimuli.text:
Tap, tap, tap on the roof at night,
The rain comes down with all its might.
It drums on the porch and the old tin pail,
It sings on the leaves and the garden rail.

Tap, tap, tap, it will not stop,
It drips from the gutter, drop by drop.
I pull up my blanket and close my eyes,
And the rain plays on till the sun will rise.

stimuli.title: How to Grow a Bean in a Cup
stimuli.text:
You can watch a seed sprout right on your windowsill. Here is how.

1. Fold a paper towel and press it against the inside of a clear plastic cup.
2. Slide a dry bean seed between the paper towel and the cup.
3. Pour a little water into the bottom of the cup so the paper towel gets wet.
4. Set the cup in a sunny window.
5. Check the cup each day and add water if the towel feels dry.

In about a week, you should see a tiny root grow down and a green shoot grow up.

stimuli.title: The Missing Sock (a play scene)
stimuli.text:
CAST: OMAR, a boy of eight. NADIA, his older sister.

(A messy bedroom. OMAR is on his knees, looking under the bed.)

OMAR: I have one blue sock. Where is the other one?

NADIA: (leaning in the doorway) Did you check the laundry basket?

OMAR: Twice! (He sits back and crosses his arms.)

NADIA: (pointing at his foot and laughing) Omar, look down.

(OMAR looks at his foot. He is wearing the other blue sock.)

stimuli.title: The First Airplane Flight
stimuli.text:
For hundreds of years, people dreamed of flying like birds. Two brothers from Ohio, Orville and Wilbur Wright, decided to make that dream come true.

The brothers owned a bicycle shop. They used what they knew about building bikes to design a flying machine. They tested gliders for several years. Then, on December 17, 1903, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville flew their airplane for 12 seconds. It was the first powered airplane flight in history. Later that day, Wilbur flew for almost a full minute.

stimuli.title: The Rainy Walk Home
stimuli.text:
The bell rang, and rain poured down outside. Jaylen had his big green umbrella. Next to him, the new student, Ana, had only a thin jacket. She held her backpack over her head.

Jaylen looked at the sky. Then he looked at Ana. "Here," he said, holding out the umbrella. "You live farther than I do. I can run home fast."

Ana smiled. "Are you sure?"

"I'm sure," said Jaylen. He pulled up his hood and dashed into the rain.

stimuli.title: The Long Trip of the Monarch Butterfly
stimuli.text:
**A Butterfly on the Move**

Every fall, millions of orange and black monarch butterflies leave the United States and Canada. Many of them fly south to the mountains of central Mexico. Some travel as far as 3,000 miles. That is a very long trip for an insect that weighs less than a paper clip.

**Why Monarchs Fly South**

Monarchs cannot live through a cold northern winter. In the mountain forests of Mexico, the air stays cool but not freezing. The butterflies cluster together on the branches of fir trees. So many monarchs gather that the branches bend under their weight.

**A Special Generation**

Most monarchs live only a few weeks. The monarchs that hatch at the end of summer are different. They can live for about eight months, long enough to make the trip south, rest all winter and start the trip back in spring.

**How People Can Help**

Monarch caterpillars eat only one kind of plant, called milkweed. When fields and roadsides are cleared, milkweed disappears, and monarchs have fewer places to lay their eggs. Many families and schools now plant milkweed in their gardens. Each new patch gives monarchs a place to rest and raise the next generation.

stimuli.title: The Snow Fort
stimuli.text:
Wind whistled across the frozen field behind Sam's house. It had snowed all night, and now the snow came up past Sam's boots. The sky was gray, and the trees were bare.

Sam and his cousin Priya grabbed two shovels. By lunchtime they had built a snow fort with walls as high as their shoulders. Inside, out of the wind, it felt almost warm.

stimuli.title: Where Does a Puddle Go?
stimuli.text:
After a rainstorm, the playground is covered with puddles. By the next afternoon, most of them are gone. Where did the water go?

The sun warms the water in the puddle. Tiny bits of water rise into the air as a gas you cannot see. This is called **evaporation**. On a hot, sunny day, puddles dry up quickly. On a cool, cloudy day, they last much longer.

Caption under the photo: A puddle in the morning (left) and the same spot in the afternoon (right).

stimuli.title: Mia's Bean Patch
stimuli.text:
Mia had never grown anything before. When Mrs. Ortiz gave each student a small square in the school garden, Mia planted six bean seeds and waited.

Every morning she ran outside before the bell. Every morning the dirt looked exactly the same. On the fourth day, she stomped back to class. "My seeds are broken," she told her friend Theo. "Nothing is happening."

Theo shrugged. "Maybe they are busy underground."

Mia did not believe him. That afternoon she almost dug the seeds up to check. Mrs. Ortiz knelt beside her. "Seeds need water, sun and time," she said. "You have given them two of those. The third one is the hardest."

So Mia made a plan. She drew a chart on a card and taped it to her desk. Each day she watered her patch and drew a small circle on the chart. She did not dig. She did not peek under the dirt.

On the ninth day, a tiny green loop pushed up through the soil. By the next week, five more had joined it. Mia added a star to her chart for every sprout, and she showed Theo each one.

When her little brother planted sunflower seeds at home and complained that they were not growing, Mia smiled at him. "Give them water, sun and time," she said. "The third one is the hardest."

stimuli.title: Why Leaves Change Color
stimuli.text:
In summer, most tree leaves are green. They are green because of chlorophyll, a material that helps leaves use sunlight to make food for the tree.

In the fall, the days grow shorter and cooler. Many trees stop making chlorophyll. As the green fades away, other colors that were hiding in the leaf begin to show. That is why the leaves of many trees turn yellow and orange. Soon after, the leaves fall to the ground, and the tree rests for the winter.

stimuli.title: Grandpa's Early Morning
stimuli.text:
Every Saturday, Grandpa Lee woke up before the sun. He filled a thermos with tea and walked to the lake with his fishing pole. He did not care much about catching fish. Most days he let them go.

"Then why do you get up so early?" asked his granddaughter, Kim.

Grandpa smiled. "At dawn, the lake is quiet. The birds wake up one by one. It is the most peaceful hour of the whole week."

stimuli.title: We Need a Bike Lane on Elm Street
stimuli.text:
Many students in our town ride their bikes to Elm Street School. Right now, they must ride next to busy cars and trucks. This is not safe.

Our town should paint a bike lane on Elm Street. A bike lane would give riders their own space on the road. Drivers would know where to watch for bikes. More families might choose to ride instead of drive, which would mean less traffic in the morning. A bike lane is a simple way to keep children safe.

stimuli.title: The Lemonade Stand
stimuli.text:
Rosa wanted to buy a new library book bag. First, she asked her dad if she could sell lemonade. He said yes. Next, she squeezed a big bowl of lemons and stirred in sugar and water. Then she made a sign that said "Cold Lemonade" and set up a table by the sidewalk.

At first, nobody stopped. After a while, a mail carrier bought a cup. Soon, a whole soccer team lined up. By evening, Rosa had sold every cup.

stimuli.title: Frogs and Toads
stimuli.text:
Frogs and toads look alike, but they are not the same. Both are amphibians, and both lay their eggs in water. Both eat insects.

There are also differences. Most frogs have smooth, wet skin, while most toads have dry, bumpy skin. Frogs usually have long back legs for big jumps. Toads have shorter legs, so they take small hops or walk. Frogs tend to stay near water, but toads can live in drier places, such as gardens and fields.

stimuli.title: My First Swim Meet
stimuli.text:
I stood on the edge of the pool, and my knees would not stop shaking. The other swimmers looked so tall. When the whistle blew, I dove in and kicked as hard as I could.

I did not win. I came in fourth out of six. But when I climbed out, my coach gave me a high five. "You beat your best time," she said. I grinned all the way home.

stimuli.title: Built for the Desert
stimuli.text:
Camels are very well suited to life in the hot, dry desert. A camel's hump does not hold water, as many people think. Instead, it stores fat that the camel can use for energy when food is hard to find.

Camels have long, thick eyelashes that keep blowing sand out of their eyes. They can close their nostrils during a sandstorm. Their wide, padded feet keep them from sinking into soft sand, the way snowshoes help a person walk on snow.

stimuli.title: Two Builders
stimuli.text:
Ben and Luis each built a block tower for the class contest. Ben built fast. He stacked the blocks as high as he could and did not check if they were straight. Luis built slowly. He tested each block before he set the next one on top.

When Ms. Park bumped the table, Ben's tower crashed to the floor. Luis's tower wobbled, but it stayed standing.

stimuli.title: Two Texts About Sea Turtles
stimuli.text:
Text 1: Sea turtles spend almost their whole lives in the ocean. But every few years, a female swims to a sandy beach at night. She digs a hole, lays her eggs and covers them with sand. About two months later, the baby turtles hatch and crawl toward the water.

Text 2: Many beach towns now ask people to turn off outdoor lights near the shore at night. Baby sea turtles find the ocean by heading toward the brightest light. Bright lights from houses can make them crawl the wrong way. Volunteers also put fences around nests so people do not step on them.

stimuli.title: The Beaver and the Otter
stimuli.text:
All summer, Beaver cut branches and packed mud into her dam. Otter floated on his back in the sun. "Come and play!" Otter called. "There is plenty of time."

"Winter is coming," said Beaver, and she kept working.

When the ice came, Beaver's lodge was warm and dry, with a pile of branches to eat. Otter shivered on the cold bank. Beaver called him inside and shared her food. Otter said, "Next summer, I will help you build."

stimuli.title: Tiny Flyers
stimuli.text:
Hummingbirds are the smallest birds in the world. Some are not much bigger than your thumb. Their wings beat dozens of times each second, which makes the humming sound that gives them their name.

Hummingbirds can fly in ways most birds cannot. They can hover in one spot like a helicopter. They can even fly backward. A hummingbird uses its long, thin beak to drink sweet nectar from flowers. It must eat often, because flying this way uses a great deal of energy.

stimuli.title: The Broken Kite
stimuli.text:
Kofi's kite string snapped, and the kite landed in a tall tree. His friends said, "Forget it. Let's go play ball."

Kofi did not give up. He asked the park ranger for help. When the ranger said she had no ladder, Kofi found a long stick and tried to reach it. That did not work either. Finally, he waited for a gust of wind. The kite slid off the branch, and Kofi caught it in his arms.

stimuli.title: The Parts of a Plant
stimuli.text:
Every part of a plant has a job. The roots grow under the ground. They hold the plant in place and take in water. The stem carries that water up to the leaves. The leaves use sunlight to make food for the plant. The flower makes seeds that can grow into new plants.

Diagram: A drawing of a sunflower. Lines point to four labels: roots at the bottom, stem in the middle, leaves on the sides and flower at the top.

stimuli.title: The Old Oak
stimuli.text:
The old oak stands beside the school,
Its branches wide, its shadow cool.
In spring it wears a coat of green,
The brightest green I've ever seen.

In fall it drops its leaves of gold,
They crunch beneath us, crisp and old.
In winter, bare, it waits for May,
And dreams of children at their play.

stimuli.title: Sally Ride Reaches Space
stimuli.text:
When Sally Ride was a girl, she loved science and tennis. She studied hard and became a scientist.

In 1978, NASA chose her to train as an astronaut. Five years later, in June 1983, she flew into space on the space shuttle Challenger. She became the first American woman to travel to space. Later in her life, Sally Ride started programs to help girls and boys explore science. She wanted every child to know that they could reach for the stars.

stimuli.title: The Class Pet (a play scene)
stimuli.text:
CAST: MR. BELL, a teacher. HANA and DEV, two students. PEANUT, a hamster (not seen).

(A classroom. A cage sits on a table by the window. The cage door is open.)

HANA: (gasping) Mr. Bell! Peanut's cage is empty!

DEV: (dropping to the floor) I'll look under the desks.

MR. BELL: Everyone stay calm, and please walk carefully.

(A rustling sound comes from the art supply box. DEV tiptoes over and lifts the lid.)

DEV: Found him! He's sleeping in the cotton balls.

stimuli.title: The Water Cycle
stimuli.text:
The water on Earth is used again and again. This is called the water cycle.

First, the sun heats water in oceans, lakes and rivers. The water turns into a gas and rises into the sky. Next, the gas cools high in the air and turns into tiny drops that form clouds. When the drops in a cloud grow heavy, they fall as rain or snow. Finally, the water runs into rivers, lakes and oceans, and the cycle begins again.

stimuli.title: The Science Fair
stimuli.text:
Grace stayed up late every night for a week. She tested which kind of paper towel soaked up the most water. She measured each one three times and wrote the numbers in a notebook.

Her friend Lily asked, "Why are you working so hard? It's only the school fair."

Grace held up her notebook. "I want to be a scientist someday," she said. "Real scientists check their work more than once."

stimuli.title: Day and Night
stimuli.text:
Have you ever wondered why the sun seems to rise in the morning and set at night? The sun does not really move across the sky. Instead, Earth is spinning.

Earth spins like a top, making one full turn about every 24 hours. When your side of Earth faces the sun, it is daytime. As Earth keeps turning, your side moves away from the sun, and it becomes night. At that same moment, it is daytime on the other side of the world.

stimuli.title: Twin Sisters
stimuli.text:
Maya and Mira are twins, but they are very different. Maya loves to talk. She tells jokes at dinner and makes new friends everywhere she goes. Mira is quiet. She would rather read a book in a corner than go to a party.

But both sisters love animals. On Saturdays, they help at the animal shelter together. Maya talks to the visitors, and Mira gently brushes the shy cats.

stimuli.title: Every School Needs a Garden
stimuli.text:
I believe every school should have a garden. When students grow their own vegetables, they are more willing to taste them. A garden is also a great place to learn science. Students can see how seeds sprout, how bees visit flowers and how plants need water and sun.

Gardens teach teamwork, too. Someone has to water, someone has to pull weeds and someone has to pick the tomatoes. A school garden does not need much space. Even a few large pots can make a big difference.

stimuli.title: Biscuit Comes Home
stimuli.text:
I knew something was wrong the moment I opened the back door. The gate was swinging in the wind, and Biscuit, our little brown dog, was gone.

My mom and I walked up and down every street on our block. We called his name until our voices were scratchy. My little sister, Zoe, cried so hard that she got the hiccups. That night, I could not fall asleep. I kept looking at Biscuit's empty bed by the heater.

The next morning I had an idea. I made twenty posters with Biscuit's picture and our phone number. Zoe colored a red heart on each one. We taped them to light poles, the library window and the bulletin board at the grocery store.

All day the phone stayed quiet. Then, just after dinner, it rang. A woman named Mrs. Adeyemi said a small brown dog was sleeping on her porch two streets away. He had a red collar with a bell.

We ran the whole way. When Biscuit saw us, his tail wagged so fast that his whole body wiggled. Zoe hugged him, and this time she cried happy tears.

Now I check the gate latch every single day. I also keep one extra poster in my desk, just in case a neighbor ever loses a pet.

stimuli.title: The Pony Express
stimuli.text:
**Mail Moves Slowly**

In the 1850s, many Americans moved west to California. Sending a letter from the eastern states to California could take weeks or even months. People wanted a faster way to get news.

**A Bold Plan**

In April 1860, a company started the Pony Express. Young riders carried mail on horseback from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California. That route was almost 2,000 miles long. Along the way stood small stations where a rider could jump onto a fresh horse and gallop on. A letter that once took weeks could now arrive in about ten days.

**Riding Through Danger**

The riders faced snowstorms in the mountains, burning heat in the deserts and rivers they had to cross. Most riders were light so the horses could run fast. Each rider carried the mail in a leather cover that fit over the saddle and could be moved quickly to the next horse.

**The End of the Trail**

In October 1861, workers finished a telegraph line that stretched all the way across the country. A telegraph message traveled over wires in minutes, not days. The Pony Express was no longer needed, and it closed after only about eighteen months. Even so, people still remember the brave riders who carried the mail west.

stimuli.title: The Desert Hike
stimuli.text:
The sun blazed over the red rocks of the canyon. There were no trees for shade, only small, dusty bushes and a few tall cactus plants. By noon, the ground was so hot that Eli could feel it through his sneakers.

"Drink some water," said his aunt. "Out here, the heat is the biggest danger." Eli took a long sip and pulled his hat lower. They decided to rest in the shadow of a big rock until the afternoon cooled.

stimuli.title: A Cleaner Park
stimuli.text:
Last spring, Maple Park was full of litter. Wrappers blew across the grass, and bottles sat under the benches. The students at Lincoln School wanted to fix it.

First, they counted the trash cans in the park. There were only two. The students wrote a letter to the town council asking for more cans. The council added six new ones. Then the students painted signs that said "Keep Our Park Clean." By summer, the park looked much better.

stimuli.title: The New Bike, Chapter 3
stimuli.text:
Chapter 1 told how Carlos saved his allowance for a whole year. Chapter 2 told how he finally bought a red bike but kept falling off it.

Chapter 3: Every evening, Carlos practiced in the empty parking lot. His dad held the back of the seat. On Friday, Carlos pedaled to the end of the lot and turned around. His dad was standing far away, waving. He had let go long ago, and Carlos had not even noticed.

Chapter 4 will tell about Carlos's first ride to school.

stimuli.title: Penguins in the Water
stimuli.text:
Penguins are birds, but they cannot fly. Their wings are short, stiff flippers. That might sound like a problem, but penguins are expert swimmers.

In the water, a penguin flaps its flippers to zoom forward, almost as if it were flying underwater. Its smooth body shape helps it slip through the water. Its feet and tail help it steer. Some penguins can dive deep and hold their breath for several minutes while they hunt for fish.

stimuli.title: Night Sounds
stimuli.text:
When Aiden went camping for the first time, every sound made him jump. A twig snapped, and he sat straight up. An owl hooted, and he grabbed his flashlight.

His big brother Noah laughed softly. "Those are just the woods talking," he said. He named each sound for Aiden: the owl, the frogs, the wind in the pines. Soon the sounds did not seem scary at all. Aiden fell asleep listening to the frogs sing.

stimuli.title: Inside a Volcano
stimuli.text:
A volcano is an opening in Earth's surface. Deep underground, it is so hot that some rock melts. This melted rock is called **magma**. When pressure builds up, magma pushes up through the volcano. Once it flows out onto the surface, it is called **lava**.

Glossary
magma: melted rock that is still under the ground
lava: melted rock that has come out onto Earth's surface

stimuli.title: Pancake Morning
stimuli.text:
Dad flipped a pancake so high that it stuck to the ceiling. Lucas and his sister stared up at it. For a second, nobody said a word. Then the pancake peeled off and landed, plop, right back in the pan.

Dad bowed. Lucas laughed so hard that milk came out of his nose. It was the best Sunday breakfast ever.

stimuli.title: A Library on Wheels
stimuli.text:
Not every town has a library close by. In some places, the library comes to the people instead. A bookmobile is a big truck or bus filled with shelves of books.

The bookmobile drives to neighborhoods, farms and schools on a set schedule. Readers climb aboard, pick out books and check them out with a library card. When the bookmobile returns the next week, they can bring the books back and choose new ones.

stimuli.title: Spring
stimuli.text:
Buds wake up on every tree,
Bees come buzzing, one, two, three.
Puddles shine and robins sing,
Hello, hello, it's finally spring!

Kites go up and boots come off,
No more sniffles, no more cough.
Grass grows green and flowers ring,
Hello, hello, it's finally spring!

stimuli.title: Lightning and Thunder
stimuli.text:
During a storm, you see a flash of lightning first. A few seconds later, you hear the boom of thunder. But lightning and thunder actually happen at the same time.

You see the lightning first because light travels much faster than sound. The light reaches your eyes almost right away. The sound takes longer to reach your ears. The farther away the storm is, the longer you have to wait between the flash and the boom.

stimuli.title: The Star Jar
stimuli.text:
Every night before bed, Leah wrote one good thing about her day on a paper star. She folded it and dropped it into a glass jar.

On her birthday, the jar was full. Leah poured out all the stars and read them one by one. There was the day she learned to whistle, the day her cousin visited and the day she found a ladybug. "I had a lot of good days," she said.

stimuli.title: Life in a Beehive
stimuli.text:
A honeybee hive is a busy place. Thousands of bees live and work together, and each one has a job.

Every hive has one queen bee. Her main job is to lay eggs, and she can lay more than a thousand in a single day. Most of the other bees are worker bees, and they are all female. Young workers clean the hive and feed the babies. Older workers fly out to gather nectar and pollen from flowers.

When a worker finds a good patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and does a special dance. The way she moves tells the other bees which way to fly and how far to go. Back in the hive, the bees turn nectar into honey, which they store in wax cells to eat during the winter.

stimuli.title: The Library Helper
stimuli.text:
Every Tuesday after school, Ruby helped Mr. Kim at the town library. Her job was to put returned books back on the shelves. At first, she thought the job was boring. The books were heavy, and the shelves were tall.

One Tuesday, a small boy came to the desk. He was looking for a book about whales but could not find one. Ruby knew just where the ocean books were because she had shelved them that morning. She walked him to the right row and pulled out a big book with a blue whale on the cover.

The boy hugged the book. "This is the best one!" he said.

After that, Ruby did not think her job was boring. She started learning where every kind of book lived, so she could help the next reader too.

stimuli.title: Lewis and Clark
stimuli.text:
In 1803, the United States bought a huge area of land in the West. President Thomas Jefferson asked Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore it.

In May 1804, their group set out from near St. Louis. They traveled up the Missouri River by boat. A Shoshone woman named Sacagawea joined them and helped them speak with Native American groups they met. In November 1805, the group finally reached the Pacific Ocean. They returned home in 1806 with maps and notes about plants and animals.

stimuli.title: The Young Fox
stimuli.text:
A young fox found a grape vine growing on a high wall. She jumped and jumped but could not reach the grapes. Instead of walking away, she rolled a log to the wall, climbed on top and picked a bunch.

An old fox watched her. "When I was young," he said, "I would have said those grapes were sour and left. You have taught me something today."

stimuli.title: Why Recess Matters
stimuli.text:
Some schools have cut recess time to make more room for lessons. That is a mistake.

Children need time to run, jump and play outside. After recess, many students find it easier to sit still and pay attention in class. Recess is also when children learn to share, take turns and solve problems with friends. A few minutes of play can help the rest of the school day go better for everyone.

questions.stem: What is the value of the 6 in 3,682?
questions.explanation: The 6 is in the hundreds place, so it means 6 hundreds, or 600. It is not in the tens place; that digit is the 8.

questions.stem: Ava started reading at 3:15 p.m. She read for 40 minutes. What time did she stop?
questions.explanation: Count on 40 minutes from 3:15: 3:15 plus 40 minutes is 3:55 p.m. It is not 4:55, because less than one hour went by.

questions.stem: Which expression shows 4 groups of 6 apples?
questions.explanation: 4 equal groups of 6 is 4 × 6, which is 24 apples. The expression 4 + 6 only adds one group of each.

questions.stem: How many sides does a pentagon have?
questions.explanation: A pentagon has 5 sides and 5 angles. A hexagon has 6 sides and an octagon has 8.

questions.stem: Round 4,372 to the nearest hundred:
questions.explanation: Look at the tens digit, 7. It is 5 or more, so round the hundreds up from 4,300 to 4,400. 4,370 is rounded to the nearest ten instead.

questions.stem: A garden is shaped like a rectangle. It is 7 meters long and 6 meters wide. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area is length times width: 7 x 6 = 42 square meters. 26 is the perimeter, the distance around.

questions.stem: In 7 × n = 56, what number is n? Type the number.
questions.explanation: 7 × 8 = 56, so n is 8. You can also think 56 ÷ 7 = 8.

questions.stem: Maya's class read 1,248 pages in October and 965 pages in November. How many pages did they read in all?
questions.explanation: 1,248 + 965 = 2,213. If you forget to carry the 1 into the hundreds, you get 2,113.

questions.stem: Liam has 3 quarters, 2 dimes and 4 pennies. How much money does he have?
questions.explanation: 3 quarters are 75 cents, 2 dimes are 20 cents and 4 pennies are 4 cents. 75 + 20 + 4 = 99 cents. 9 is only the number of coins.

questions.stem: Which expression has the same product as 3 × 8?
questions.explanation: You can multiply in either order and get the same product, so 8 × 3 = 24, just like 3 × 8. The expression 3 + 8 is 11.

questions.stem: A shape has 4 sides that are all the same length, but it has no right angles. What is the best name for this shape?
questions.explanation: A rhombus has 4 equal sides. A square also has 4 equal sides, but a square must have 4 right angles.

questions.stem: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. Leo eats 1 slice. What fraction of the pizza did he eat?
questions.explanation: Leo ate 1 of 8 equal parts, so he ate 1/8. The fraction 7/8 is the part that is left.

questions.stem: A rug is a rectangle 9 feet long and 5 feet wide. What is the perimeter of the rug?
questions.explanation: Add all four sides: 9 + 5 + 9 + 5 = 28 feet. 14 feet counts only two sides, and 45 is the area.

questions.stem: Which comparison is true?
questions.explanation: 45,091 and 45,019 match until the tens place, where 9 tens is more than 1 ten. In 38,207 and 38,270, the 7 tens make 38,270 the larger one.

questions.stem: Ben has 35 marbles. He puts the same number in each of 5 bags. How many marbles are in each bag?
questions.explanation: 35 ÷ 5 = 7, because 5 × 7 = 35. The number 30 comes from subtracting, which is not how you share.

questions.passage:
A bar graph shows the favorite fruit of students in a class.

| Fruit | Students |
|---|---|
| Apples | 8 |
| Bananas | 5 |
| Grapes | 11 |
| Oranges | 6 |
questions.stem: How many more students chose grapes than bananas? Type the number.
questions.explanation: Grapes have 11 students and bananas have 5. 11 - 5 = 6 more students.

questions.stem: A rectangle is cut into 6 equal parts. What fraction of the whole rectangle is one part?
questions.explanation: One part out of 6 equal parts is 1/6 of the whole. 6/6 would be all of the parts.

questions.stem: A school library had 5,000 books. It gave away 1,326 books. How many books are left? Type the number.
questions.explanation: 5,000 - 1,326 = 3,674. Regroup across the zeros: 5,000 is the same as 4,990 + 10.

questions.stem: Rosa buys 3 notebooks for \$4 each and a pen for \$2. She pays with a \$20 bill. How much change does she get?
questions.explanation: The notebooks cost 3 × \$4 = \$12, and with the pen that is \$14. Then \$20 - \$14 = \$6. Forgetting the pen gives \$8.

questions.stem: What is 23 × 46?
questions.explanation: 23 × 40 = 920 and 23 × 6 = 138. Add them: 920 + 138 = 1,058. Stopping at 920 forgets the ones part.

questions.stem: Which two measurements are equal to 1 yard? Choose two.
questions.explanation: 1 yard is 3 feet, and each foot is 12 inches, so 1 yard is 36 inches. 12 inches is only 1 foot.

questions.stem: Which two numbers are factors of 24? Choose two.
questions.explanation: 6 × 4 = 24 and 8 × 3 = 24, so 6 and 8 are factors. The number 48 is a multiple of 24, not a factor.

questions.stem: Which two fractions are equal to 2/3? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Multiply the top and bottom of 2/3 by the same number: by 2 gives 4/6 and by 4 gives 8/12. The fraction 6/8 equals 3/4, not 2/3.

questions.stem: How many lines of symmetry does a square have? Type the number.
questions.explanation: A square folds onto itself along 2 lines through the middles of opposite sides and along its 2 diagonals. That is 4 lines.

questions.stem: A pitcher holds 2 liters of juice. How many milliliters is that?
questions.explanation: 1 liter is 1,000 milliliters, so 2 liters is 2 x 1,000 = 2,000 mL.

questions.stem: Which number is prime?
questions.explanation: 29 has only two factors, 1 and 29. The others are composite: 21 = 3 × 7, 27 = 3 × 9 and 39 = 3 × 13.

questions.stem: Which decimal is the same as 47/100?
questions.explanation: 47 hundredths is written 0.47. The number 4.7 means 47 tenths, which is ten times as much.

questions.stem: Angle ABC is made of two smaller angles that do not overlap. One measures 35 degrees and the other measures 48 degrees. What is the measure of angle ABC?
questions.explanation: When angles do not overlap, add them: 35 + 48 = 83 degrees. 13 degrees comes from subtracting instead of adding.

questions.stem: What is 158 ÷ 6?
questions.explanation: 6 × 26 = 156, and 158 - 156 = 2, so the answer is 26 R 2. A remainder of 8 cannot be right, because it is bigger than 6.

questions.stem: 27 students are going on a trip. Each van holds 6 students. How many vans are needed so every student has a seat?
questions.explanation: 27 ÷ 6 = 4 R 3. Four vans carry 24 students, and the 3 left over need one more van, so 5 vans.

questions.stem: A triangle has angles of 90 degrees, 45 degrees and 45 degrees. Which two names describe this triangle? Choose two.
questions.explanation: It has a 90 degree angle, so it is a right triangle. Two equal angles mean two equal sides, so it is also isosceles.

questions.stem: The school play began at 6:45 p.m. and ended at 8:20 p.m. How long was the play?
questions.explanation: From 6:45 to 7:45 is 1 hour. From 7:45 to 8:20 is 35 more minutes. So the play lasted 1 hour 35 minutes.

questions.stem: Which list shows the decimals from least to greatest?
questions.explanation: Write each with three places: 0.305, 0.350 and 0.503. Then 305 < 350 < 503. A longer decimal like 0.305 is not bigger just because it has more digits.

questions.stem: What is the value of 3 × (8 + 2) - 4?
questions.explanation: Do the parentheses first: 8 + 2 = 10. Then 3 × 10 = 30, and 30 - 4 = 26. Skipping the parentheses gives 3 × 8 + 2 - 4 = 22.

questions.stem: A box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide and 5 cm tall. What is the volume of the box?
questions.explanation: Volume is length x width x height: 4 x 3 x 5 = 60 cubic centimeters. 12 uses only the length and width.

questions.stem: What is 1/2 + 1/3?
questions.explanation: Use sixths: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6, so the sum is 5/6. Adding the tops and the bottoms to get 2/5 does not work.

questions.stem: On a coordinate grid, point P is at (3, 5) and point Q is at (3, 9). How many units apart are the two points? Type the number.
questions.explanation: Both points have x = 3, so they are on the same vertical gridline. Subtract the y values: 9 - 5 = 4 units.

questions.stem: Pattern A starts at 0 and adds 3 each time. Pattern B starts at 0 and adds 6 each time. When Pattern A reaches 12, what is the matching term in Pattern B? Type the number.
questions.explanation: Pattern A goes 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 and Pattern B goes 0, 6, 12, 18, 24. The fifth terms are 12 and 24, and each B term is twice the A term.

questions.passage:
Ana measured her ribbons and made a line plot. Each X is one ribbon.

| Length (inch) | Ribbons |
|---|---|
| 1/4 | X X X |
| 1/2 | X X |
| 3/4 | X X X X |
questions.stem: What is the total length of all the ribbons that are 3/4 inch long?
questions.explanation: There are 4 ribbons that are 3/4 inch long. 4 x 3/4 = 12/4, which is 3 inches. 12 inches forgets that each piece is a fourth.

questions.stem: Ana uses 3/4 cup of flour for one batch of muffins. How many cups of flour does she need for 4 batches? Type the number.
questions.explanation: 4 × 3/4 = 12/4, and 12/4 = 3. She needs 3 cups.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. Maya was so "famished" after soccer practice that she ate two sandwiches. What does "famished" mean?
questions.explanation: Maya ate two sandwiches, which is a clue that she was very hungry. Being tired would not make her eat so much.

questions.stem: What is the lesson of the fable?
options: Acorns are the best winter food
questions.explanation: Squirrel rushes and drops acorns, while Snail carries one at a time and ends with more. Squirrel is faster, but that is a detail, not the lesson.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of "The Amazing Octopus"?
options: An octopus can squirt dark ink
The ocean is home to many animals
An octopus has eight long arms
questions.explanation: The whole article lists unusual things about the octopus, like three hearts, no bones and color changes. Squirting ink is one of those details, not the main idea.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. Leo had to "reread" the directions to understand them. What does "reread" mean?
questions.explanation: The prefix re- means "again," so reread means to read again. The prefix pre- would mean "before."

questions.stem: Which pair of words from the poem rhyme?
questions.explanation: Night and might end with the same sound, so they rhyme. Roof and rain begin with the same sound, but they do not rhyme.

questions.stem: What should a reader do right after sliding the bean into the cup?
options: Set the cup in a sunny window
Fold a paper towel in the cup
Check the cup for a green shoot
Pour a little water in the cup
questions.explanation: Step 3, pouring water into the cup, comes right after step 2. Folding the paper towel happens before the bean goes in.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. The old flashlight was "useless" because it had no batteries. What does "useless" mean?
questions.explanation: The suffix -less means "without," so useless means having no use. The suffix -ful would mean "full of."

questions.stem: Which part of the play scene is a stage direction?
options: Did you check the laundry basket?
questions.explanation: Stage directions are in parentheses and tell the actors how to move. The other choices are lines the characters say out loud.

questions.stem: How did owning a bicycle shop help the Wright brothers?
options: It paid for a trip to Ohio
It taught them to fly gliders
It helped them design a plane
It gave them a place to land
questions.explanation: The article says the brothers used what they knew about building bikes to design their flying machine. They learned about flying by testing gliders, not from the shop.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. The pitcher threw the ball, and Sam swung the "bat." Which meaning of "bat" is used in the sentence?
options: a stick for hitting a ball
questions.explanation: Sam swung it at a ball, so the bat is a stick for hitting. A flying animal is another meaning of bat, but it does not fit here.

questions.stem: The word "telescope" has the Greek root "tele." What does "tele" mean?
questions.explanation: A telescope helps you see things that are far away, and the root tele means far. Graph is the root that means to write.

questions.stem: Which word best describes Jaylen?
questions.explanation: Jaylen gives his umbrella to Ana so she stays dry, which is a generous thing to do. He does not forget anything; he makes a choice.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the article?
options: Monarchs travel far, and people can help
Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed plants
Fir trees grow in the mountains of Mexico
Most butterflies live for only a few weeks
questions.explanation: The article tells about the monarchs' long trip and ends with how people can help them. Milkweed is an important detail, but it is not what the whole article is about.

questions.stem: According to the article, why do monarchs fly south in the fall?
options: They want to find milkweed to eat
They are chased away by birds
They cannot survive a cold winter
They need to lay eggs in fir trees
questions.explanation: The section "Why Monarchs Fly South" says monarchs cannot live through a cold northern winter. The article does not say they lay eggs in fir trees.

questions.stem: Which heading would help a reader find out how long the late-summer monarchs live?
questions.explanation: The section "A Special Generation" tells that monarchs hatched at the end of summer live about eight months. The other sections are about the trip and about milkweed.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the last section, "How People Can Help"?
options: To explain why monarchs are orange
To describe the forests in Mexico
To tell how far monarchs can fly
To show how readers can help
questions.explanation: The last section tells how planting milkweed gives monarchs places to rest and lay eggs, so readers learn how they can help. How far monarchs fly is told in the first section.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. The hikers were "weary" after climbing the steep hill all day. Which two words mean almost the same as "weary"? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Climbing a steep hill all day makes people tired and worn out. Eager and cheerful describe people full of energy.

questions.stem: When and where does the story take place?
questions.explanation: The story tells about a frozen field, deep snow and bare trees, which happen in winter. The fort is built outside, not in a gym.

questions.stem: Why is the word evaporation in bold print in the article?
options: It is an important science word
It is the name of the playground
It is the title of the article
It is a word the author made up
questions.explanation: Authors use bold print to point out key words that readers should learn. Evaporation is the science word for water rising into the air as a gas.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. The puppy was "timid" and hid behind the couch when guests came. Which word means almost the same as "timid"?
questions.explanation: The puppy hid from the guests, so it was shy. Brave means the opposite of timid.

questions.stem: What lesson does Mia learn in the story?
questions.explanation: Mia wants her seeds to grow right away, but she learns that she must wait. Sun matters too, but the lesson of the story is about being patient.

questions.stem: How does Mia feel on the fourth day of waiting?
options: Proud of her tidy bean patch
questions.explanation: Mia stomps back to class and says her seeds are broken. Those actions show she is frustrated and does not want to wait.

questions.stem: How does Mia stop herself from digging up the seeds?
options: She asks Theo to dig them
She moves her patch into the sun
questions.explanation: Mia draws a chart and marks it each day when she waters. Her little brother plants the sunflower seeds, not Mia.

questions.stem: Why is the last part of the story, about Mia's little brother, important?
options: It tells how Mia met Theo
It explains how to plant beans
questions.explanation: Mia repeats her teacher's words to her brother, so the ending shows she now understands the lesson. Nothing in that part says sunflowers grow fast.

questions.stem: What causes many leaves to turn yellow and orange in the fall?
options: The leaves fall to the ground
questions.explanation: When trees stop making chlorophyll, the green fades and the hidden yellow and orange colors show. Leaves fall after they change color, so falling is not the cause.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. Kenji's little sister was "as busy as a bee" all morning in the garden. What does this simile tell the reader?
questions.explanation: Bees are always moving and working, so the simile means she kept working hard. It does not mean she was near real bees.

questions.stem: Why does Grandpa Lee go to the lake so early?
options: He wants to catch many fish
He needs to buy some tea
He wants to wake the birds
questions.explanation: Grandpa says dawn is the most peaceful hour of the week. He lets most fish go, so catching fish is not his reason.

questions.stem: What is the author's main purpose for writing "We Need a Bike Lane on Elm Street"?
options: To convince the town to add a bike lane
To explain how to ride a bike safely
To describe the trucks on Elm Street
To tell a story about a school bike race
questions.explanation: The author says the town should paint a bike lane and gives reasons, so the purpose is to persuade. The article does not teach how to ride a bike.

questions.stem: Read the sentences. Ava studied her spelling words every night. When the test came, it was "a piece of cake." What does "a piece of cake" mean here?
questions.explanation: Ava studied hard, so the test felt very easy. The idiom is not about real cake, so sweet does not fit.

questions.passage:
**light**

(noun) 1. brightness that lets you see. 2. a lamp.

(adjective) 3. not heavy. 4. pale in color.
questions.stem: Read the dictionary entry and this sentence: The box of pillows was "light," so Omar carried it by himself. Which meaning of "light" is used in the sentence?
questions.explanation: Omar could carry the box alone because it was not heavy. A pale color would not make a box easy to carry.

questions.stem: What does Rosa do right after she squeezes the lemons?
questions.explanation: The word Then shows that making the sign comes next. Asking her dad happens before she squeezes the lemons.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the information in "Frogs and Toads"?
options: By telling events in time order
By naming a problem and a fix
By listing the steps of a task
questions.explanation: The author tells how frogs and toads are alike and then how they are different. That is a compare and contrast structure.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. On the cold winter morning, the frozen lake was "a sheet of glass." What does the metaphor tell you about the lake?
options: It was made of real glass.
questions.explanation: The metaphor compares the ice to glass to show it was smooth and slick. The lake was not really made of glass.

questions.stem: Who is telling this story?
questions.explanation: The words I and my show that a character in the story is telling it, and that character swims in the race. The coach is talked about, not telling.

questions.stem: Which two details support the idea that camels are suited to the desert? Choose two.
options: Wide feet do not sink in sand
Many people think humps hold water
Snowshoes help people walk on snow
Deserts are hot and dry places
questions.explanation: Eyelashes that block sand and feet that stay on top of sand help camels live in the desert. The snowshoe sentence is a comparison, not a fact about camels.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. Jamal was so tired after the long race that he could only "___" to the water table. Which word best shows that he moved slowly and with great effort?
questions.explanation: To trudge means to walk slowly with heavy steps, like a tired runner. Dash means to move fast, which does not fit.

questions.stem: How is Luis different from Ben?
questions.explanation: Luis tests each block before adding the next, so he is more careful than Ben. Ben is the one who builds fast, and Ms. Park bumps the table.

questions.stem: What does Text 2 explain that Text 1 does not?
questions.explanation: Only Text 2 tells about turning off lights and putting fences around nests. Text 1 tells where turtles lay eggs and when the babies hatch.

questions.stem: The words "transport," "export," and "portable" all share the Latin root "port." What does "port" most likely mean?
questions.explanation: A portable radio is one you can carry, and to transport is to carry from place to place. Vis is the root that means to see.

questions.passage: (1) First, you need a clean jar with a lid. (2) Next, you put soil and small plants inside. (3) Then you add a little water and close the lid.
questions.stem: Maria is writing about how to make a jar garden. Which sentence would be the best topic sentence to come before sentence 1?
options: A jar garden is easy to make at home.
My aunt has a big garden with roses.
Plants need sunlight to grow tall.
Glass jars can break if you drop them.
questions.explanation: The paragraph gives steps for making a jar garden, and this sentence tells what the steps are for. The other sentences are about something else.

questions.stem: Three little ___ ran under the porch. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: The plural of mouse is mice. Mouses and mices are not words, and mouse names only one.

questions.stem: Which sentence about a trip is written correctly?
options: We drove to Denver in June.
We drove to denver in June.
We drove to Denver in june.
we drove to Denver in June.
questions.explanation: The names of cities and months always start with a capital letter, and so does the first word of a sentence.

questions.passage: (1) Our class started a recycling bin in October. (2) We put paper and plastic bottles in it every day. (3) By December, the bin had been emptied ten times. (4) Less trash went to the dump.
questions.stem: Which sentence would best conclude the paragraph about recycling?
options: October is the start of fall.
Plastic bottles come in many sizes.
Our bin helped us waste less.
Some students bring lunch from home.
questions.explanation: A good conclusion sums up the main idea, that recycling helped the class waste less. The other sentences add details that do not wrap up the paragraph.

questions.stem: Mom drove Ava and ___ to the library. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Me is used after a verb like drove. Try it alone: Mom drove me, not Mom drove I.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Where did you put my pencil.
Where did you put my pencil,
Where did you put my pencil?
Where did you put, my pencil?
questions.explanation: A sentence that asks something ends with a question mark. A period is for a sentence that tells something.

questions.passage: (1) Dogs make great pets. (2) They are loyal and love to play. (3) Many dogs can learn tricks. (4) Cats sleep for many hours a day. (5) A dog can also keep you active with daily walks.
questions.stem: Which sentence does not belong in the paragraph?
options: They are loyal and love to play.
Cats sleep for many hours a day.
A dog can also keep you active with daily walks.
questions.explanation: The paragraph is about why dogs make great pets. The sentence about cats does not tell about dogs.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
options: Yesterday we swimmed in the lake.
Yesterday we swam in the lake.
Yesterday we swim in the lake.
Yesterday we swum in the lake.
questions.explanation: Swim is an irregular verb, and its past tense is swam. Swimmed is not a word, and swum needs a helper like have.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a list?
options: We packed apples grapes, and nuts.
We packed apples, grapes, and nuts.
We packed, apples, grapes, and nuts.
We packed apples, grapes and, nuts.
questions.explanation: Commas go between the items in a list. No comma goes between packed and the first item.

questions.passage: (1) Lena wanted to plant a garden. (2) ________, she picked a sunny spot in the yard. (3) Next, she dug small holes for the seeds.
questions.stem: Which word best fills the blank in sentence 2?
questions.explanation: Picking a spot is the first step, and sentence 3 begins with Next. Finally would not make sense before Next.

questions.stem: The dogs in the yard ___ loudly. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: The subject dogs is plural, so it takes bark. Barks goes with one dog, and the words in the yard do not change that.

questions.stem: I ___ find my library card. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Can't is short for cannot. The apostrophe takes the place of the missing letters n and o.

questions.passage: (1) The kitten is small. (2) The kitten is gray.
questions.stem: Which sentence best combines sentences 1 and 2?
options: The kitten is small, it is gray.
The small kitten, the gray one.
The kitten is small and gray.
The kitten is small and is gray too.
questions.explanation: Joining the two describing words with and makes one clear sentence. Two sentences joined by only a comma is a run-on.

questions.stem: Which group of words is a complete sentence?
options: Because the bus was late again.
The bus stopped at the corner.
questions.explanation: A complete sentence has a subject and a verb and tells a whole thought. Because the bus was late again leaves you waiting for more.

questions.stem: The kids left ___ backpacks on the bus. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Their shows that something belongs to them. There tells where, and they're means they are.

questions.passage: (1) Then spread peanut butter on one slice. (2) Get two slices of bread. (3) Last, put the slices together. (4) Next, add banana slices on top of the peanut butter.
questions.stem: Which order of sentences makes the most sense for these sandwich steps?
questions.explanation: You get the bread, then spread peanut butter, next add banana on top, and last put the slices together. The banana cannot go on before the peanut butter.

questions.stem: I wanted to play outside, ___ it was raining. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: But joins two ideas that go against each other: wanting to play outside and the rain. So would mean the rain happened because of the wish.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the fair is written correctly?
questions.explanation: In a date, a comma goes between the day and the year. The month May also needs a capital letter.

questions.passage: (1) Carlos practiced the piano every day for a month. (2) ________, he still felt nervous before his recital.
questions.stem: Which word or phrase best fills the blank in sentence 2?
questions.explanation: However shows a surprise: he practiced a lot but still felt nervous. For example would mean the second sentence is an example of the first.

questions.stem: Of all the kids on the team, Leo is the ___ runner. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: When you compare more than two, add -est: fastest. Faster compares only two, and most fastest uses two comparing words.

questions.stem: Which sentence with a speaker is punctuated correctly?
questions.explanation: Quotation marks go around only the words Omar says, and a comma comes before the closing quotation mark.

questions.passage: (1) Bees are important to farmers. (2) They carry pollen from flower to flower. (3) This helps apple and cherry trees grow fruit.
questions.stem: Which sentence would best add support to the paragraph?
options: Some people are afraid of bee stings.
Bees help pumpkin plants grow too.
My favorite fruit is a red apple.
Wasps and bees can look alike.
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains how bees help farm crops grow, and pumpkins are another crop bees help. Bee stings do not show why bees matter to farmers.

questions.stem: Priya sings very ___ in the school choir. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Well is an adverb that tells how she sings. Good is an adjective that describes a noun, not an action.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a comma correctly after an opening word?
options: Yes, I can help you today.
Yes I, can help you today.
Yes I can, help you today.
Yes I can help, you today.
questions.explanation: Put a comma right after yes or no when it starts a sentence.

questions.stem: Ming wants to find out how many moons the planet Jupiter has. Which source would best help her?
options: a book of poems about stars
a map of the streets in her town
a story about a space dog
questions.explanation: A science book about planets gives facts about Jupiter. A book of poems or a made-up story would not give true facts.

questions.stem: The twins made lunch for ___. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: The reflexive pronoun for they is themselves. Theirselves and themself are not standard words.

questions.stem: Which sentence that speaks to Kim is written correctly?
questions.explanation: When you speak to someone by name, put a comma right after the name.

questions.passage: (1) The storm last night was bad. (2) Strong winds knocked down two trees on our street.
questions.stem: Which word is the most precise replacement for "bad" in sentence 1?
questions.explanation: Violent tells exactly how strong and harmful the storm was. Really bad is still vague and does not paint a clear picture.

questions.stem: The girl ___ won the spelling bee is my cousin. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Who is used for people, and here it is the subject of won. Which is used for things, and whom is not used as a subject.

questions.stem: The bird flapped ___ wings and flew away. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Its with no apostrophe shows ownership: the wings belong to the bird. It's means it is.

questions.passage: (1) The Grand Canyon is in Arizona. (2) It is about 277 miles long. (3) It is the best park ever. (4) Many people hike there each year.
questions.stem: Lucy is writing a report with only facts. Which sentence is an opinion that she should take out?
options: The Grand Canyon is in Arizona.
It is the best park ever.
Many people hike there each year.
questions.explanation: Saying something is the best is a feeling, not a fact anyone can check. The length of the canyon can be measured, so it is a fact.

questions.stem: Which sentence about a lost hat is written correctly?
options: I lost my hat I found it later.
I lost my hat, I found it later.
I lost my hat but, I found it later.
I lost my hat, but I found it later.
questions.explanation: Two complete thoughts can be joined with a comma and a word like but. A comma alone between them makes a run-on.

questions.stem: The rabbit was ___ across the yard. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Hop has a short vowel and ends in one consonant, so double the p before -ing: hopping. Hoping comes from hope, which means to wish.

questions.stem: Jada is writing a letter to the principal to ask for a new school garden. Which sentence is best for her audience?
options: Hey, you gotta give us a garden!
Say yes or we'll be so bummed.
Thank you for reading my request.
questions.explanation: A letter to a principal should be polite and formal. Words like gotta and bummed are informal, for talking with friends.

questions.stem: Which sentence about a ball is written correctly?
options: She has a red big ball.
She has a ball red big.
She has a big red ball.
She has a big ball red.
questions.explanation: In English, a size word like big comes before a color word like red, and both come before the noun.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows the title of a book written correctly?
options: I read the wind in the willows.
I read The wind in the willows.
I read The Wind in the Willows.
I read The Wind In The Willows.
questions.explanation: In a title, capitalize the first word and the important words. Short words like in and the stay lowercase unless they come first.

questions.passage: (1) Come to the Pine Street Library Book Sale! (2) Books cost only 50 cents. (3) The sale is Saturday from 9 a.m. to noon. (4) All money helps buy new books for kids.
questions.stem: What is the main purpose of this piece of writing?
options: to tell a story about a library
to explain how books are made
to get people to come to a sale
questions.explanation: The writing invites readers to the sale and gives reasons to come. It does not tell a story or explain how books are made.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the past progressive tense?
options: Ben will be reading a book.
questions.explanation: The past progressive uses was or were with an -ing verb, like was reading. Is reading happens now, in the present.

questions.stem: All five ___ coats hung by the door. Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: For a plural noun that ends in s, add only an apostrophe after the s: girls'. Girl's would show that one girl owns the coats.

questions.stem: Round 2,647 to the nearest ten:
questions.explanation: The ones digit is 7, which is 5 or more, so round 2,640 up to 2,650. 2,600 is the nearest hundred, not ten.

questions.stem: On a clock, the hour hand is just past the 9 and the minute hand points to the 4. What time is it?
questions.explanation: The minute hand on the 4 means 4 x 5 = 20 minutes. The hour hand just past the 9 means the hour is 9. So it is 9:20.

questions.stem: Which number sentence matches 18 pencils shared equally by 3 friends?
questions.explanation: Sharing equally is division: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 pencils each. The other number sentences are true, but they do not match sharing.

questions.stem: Which shape has exactly 3 sides and 3 angles?
questions.explanation: Tri means three, and a triangle has 3 sides and 3 angles. A square has 4 of each.

questions.stem: Omar has 832 stickers. He gives 457 to his sister. How many stickers does he have left?
questions.explanation: 832 - 457 = 375. Taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in each place gives 425, which is a common mistake.

questions.stem: Which is the best estimate for the mass of a pencil?
questions.explanation: A pencil is very light, about as heavy as a few paper clips, so 5 grams fits. 5 kilograms is as heavy as a big bag of flour.

questions.stem: The pattern 5, 9, 13, 17 keeps going. What is the next number?
questions.explanation: Each number is 4 more than the one before, so the next number is 17 + 4 = 21.

questions.stem: A number line from 0 to 1 is split into 4 equal parts. A dot is on the third mark after 0. What fraction does the dot show?
questions.explanation: Each part is 1/4, and the dot is 3 parts from 0, so it shows 3/4. Counting the marks as the bottom number gives 3/5 by mistake.

questions.stem: A rectangle is covered by unit squares with no gaps or overlaps. It has 3 rows with 8 squares in each row. What is its area in square units? Type the number.
questions.explanation: Count the squares by rows: 3 rows of 8 is 3 x 8 = 24 square units.

questions.stem: Kai had some shells. He found 9 more, and now he has 23. How many shells did Kai have at first? Type the number.
questions.explanation: Something + 9 = 23, so subtract: 23 - 9 = 14 shells.

questions.stem: Line AB and line CD cross and make four right angles. What kind of lines are they?
questions.explanation: Lines that cross to make right angles are perpendicular. Parallel lines never cross at all.

questions.stem: What is the value of the 4 in 2,436,105?
questions.explanation: Reading from the left, 2 is in the millions place and 4 is in the hundred thousands place, so it is worth 400,000.

questions.stem: How many cups are in 3 quarts?
questions.explanation: 1 quart is 4 cups, so 3 quarts is 3 x 4 = 12 cups. 6 cups would be using 2 cups in a quart, which is a pint.

questions.stem: A farm packs 1,235 eggs each day. How many eggs does it pack in 7 days?
questions.explanation: 1,000 × 7 = 7,000 and 235 × 7 = 1,645. Together that is 8,645 eggs.

questions.stem: Lena has 4 times as many stamps as Raj. Raj has 7 stamps. How many stamps does Lena have?
questions.explanation: 4 times as many means multiply: 4 × 7 = 28 stamps. Adding 4 + 7 = 11 is a common mistake.

questions.stem: A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 inches. Its length is 9 inches. What is its width?
questions.explanation: Length plus width is half the perimeter: 30 / 2 = 15. Then 15 - 9 = 6 inches. 12 inches is both widths together, so one width is half of 12.

questions.stem: How many faces does a rectangular prism have?
questions.explanation: A rectangular prism, like a shoe box, has a top, a bottom and 4 sides, which is 6 faces. It has 8 vertices and 12 edges.

questions.stem: Which fraction is greater than 1/2?
questions.explanation: Half of 8 is 4, and 5/8 has more than 4 eighths, so it is greater than 1/2. The fraction 3/7 is a little less than half, because half of 7 is 3.5.

questions.stem: Which two numbers are multiples of 7? Choose two.
questions.explanation: 7 × 6 = 42 and 7 × 9 = 63. Numbers like 27, 47 and 17 have a 7 in them, but 7 does not divide them evenly.

questions.stem: A baker puts 744 rolls into bags of 6. How many bags does the baker fill? Type the number.
Maya buys a book for \$6.75 and pays with a \$10 bill. How much change should she get?
questions.explanation: Subtract: \$10.00 - \$6.75 = \$3.25. Count up to check: \$6.75 plus 25 cents is \$7, and 3 more dollars makes \$10.

questions.stem: Which number is composite?
questions.explanation: 51 = 3 × 17, so it has more than two factors. The numbers 43, 47 and 53 are prime.

questions.stem: What is the value of the 8 in 3.28?
questions.explanation: The first place after the decimal point is tenths and the next is hundredths. The 8 is in the hundredths place.

questions.stem: Start at (0, 0) on a coordinate grid. Move 4 units to the right and then 2 units up. Where do you end?
questions.explanation: The first number tells how far right and the second tells how far up, so the point is (4, 2). (2, 4) mixes up the order.

questions.stem: An L-shaped patio is made of two rectangles that do not overlap. One is 6 feet by 4 feet. The other is 3 feet by 2 feet. What is the total area of the patio?
questions.explanation: Find each area and add: 6 x 4 = 24 and 3 x 2 = 6, so 24 + 6 = 30 square feet. 24 is only the bigger rectangle.

questions.stem: A garden has 6 rows with 8 tomato plants in each row. Sam moves 15 of the plants to pots. How many plants are left in the garden? Type the number.
questions.explanation: 6 × 8 = 48 plants. Then 48 - 15 = 33 plants are left.

questions.stem: Jada walked 2 1/4 miles on Monday and 1 2/4 miles on Tuesday. How far did she walk in all?
questions.explanation: Add the wholes, 2 + 1 = 3, and the fourths, 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4, for 3 3/4 miles. The bottom number stays 4, so 3 3/8 is wrong.

questions.stem: A bag of apples weighs 5 pounds. How many ounces does it weigh?
questions.explanation: 1 pound is 16 ounces, so 5 pounds is 5 x 16 = 80 ounces. 60 ounces would use 12 in a pound, which is the number of inches in a foot.

questions.stem: Which two numbers are equal to 0.6? Choose two.
questions.explanation: 0.6 is 6 tenths, which is 6/10, and 6 tenths is the same as 60 hundredths, 0.60. The numbers 0.06 and 6/100 are only 6 hundredths.

questions.stem: Which expression is equal to 6 × 14?
questions.explanation: Break 14 into 10 + 4 and multiply each part by 6: 60 + 24 = 84, which is 6 × 14. In (6 × 10) + 4 the 4 was never multiplied by 6.

questions.stem: An angle measures 130 degrees. What kind of angle is it?
questions.explanation: An obtuse angle is more than 90 degrees and less than 180 degrees, so 130 degrees is obtuse.

questions.passage:
A picture graph shows books read by a class. Each picture stands for 4 books.

| Day | Pictures |
|---|---|
| Monday | 3 |
| Tuesday | 5 |
| Wednesday | 2 |
questions.stem: How many books did the class read on Tuesday and Wednesday together?
questions.explanation: Tuesday and Wednesday have 5 + 2 = 7 pictures. Each picture is 4 books, so 7 x 4 = 28 books. 7 is only the number of pictures.

questions.stem: What is 4.5 + 2.37?
questions.explanation: Line up the decimal points: 4.50 + 2.37 = 6.87. Lining up the last digits instead gives 2.82.

questions.stem: Which expression means "add 5 and 7, then multiply by 3"?
questions.explanation: The parentheses make you add 5 and 7 first, then multiply the sum by 3. In 5 + 7 × 3 you would multiply 7 × 3 first.

questions.stem: A toy shelf is built from two rectangular boxes that do not overlap. One box is 5 in by 2 in by 3 in. The other is 4 in by 2 in by 3 in. What is the total volume?
questions.explanation: Find each volume and add: 5 x 2 x 3 = 30 and 4 x 2 x 3 = 24, so 30 + 24 = 54 cubic inches. 30 is only one box.

questions.stem: What is 2/3 × 3/5?
questions.explanation: Multiply the tops and the bottoms: 2 × 3 = 6 and 3 × 5 = 15, so 6/15, which simplifies to 2/5. Adding the tops and the bottoms gives 5/8, which is not multiplying.

questions.stem: Which two statements are always true? Choose two.
questions.explanation: A square has 4 right angles, so it is always a rectangle. A rhombus has two pairs of parallel sides, so it is always a parallelogram. A rectangle is a square only when all its sides are equal.

questions.stem: A pattern starts at 3. The rule is "multiply by 2, then subtract 1." What is the fourth term?
questions.explanation: 3, then 3 × 2 - 1 = 5, then 5 × 2 - 1 = 9, then 9 × 2 - 1 = 17. The number 9 is only the third term.

questions.stem: A straight angle measures 180 degrees. It is split into two angles. One of them measures 125 degrees. How many degrees does the other angle measure? Type the number.
questions.explanation: The two angles add up to 180 degrees, so subtract: 180 - 125 = 55 degrees.

questions.stem: Five friends share 3 sandwiches equally. How much does each friend get?
questions.explanation: Sharing 3 among 5 is 3 ÷ 5, which is 3/5. Each friend gets less than a whole sandwich, so 5/3 is too much.

questions.stem: Read the sentences. The kitchen counter was covered with crumbs and dishes. Dad asked Nora to "tidy" it before dinner. What does "tidy" mean?
questions.explanation: The counter was messy, so Dad wanted Nora to clean it up. Cooking on it would not fix the mess.

questions.stem: What lesson does Otter learn in the fable?
options: Playing in the sun is best
Winter is a time for sleep
questions.explanation: Otter plays all summer and is cold when winter comes, so he decides to help build next time. The fable does not say beavers swim well.

questions.stem: What is "Tiny Flyers" mostly about?
options: How helicopters hover in the air
Why birds need to eat often
questions.explanation: The article tells how hummingbirds hover, fly backward and beat their wings fast. Helicopters are only used as a comparison.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. The sign said the trail was "unsafe" after the big storm. What does "unsafe" mean?
questions.explanation: The prefix un- means "not," so unsafe means not safe. Safe again would need the prefix re-.

questions.stem: Which word best describes Kofi?
questions.explanation: Kofi keeps trying new ways to get his kite back after each one fails, so he is determined. He is not lazy, because he never gives up.

questions.stem: What does the diagram described below the article help a reader see?
questions.explanation: The diagram labels the roots, stem, leaves and flower on a drawing, so it shows where each part is. It does not show how tall a sunflower grows.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. The water in the pond was "shallow," so the ducks could stand in it. Which word means the opposite of "shallow"?
questions.explanation: Shallow water is not deep, which is why the ducks could stand. Muddy tells about the water's color, not how deep it is.

questions.stem: How is the poem "The Old Oak" organized?
options: By the hours of one day
By the seasons of the year
By the parts of the tree
questions.explanation: The poem moves from spring to fall to winter, so it follows the seasons. Children are mentioned once, but they do not set the order.

questions.stem: Why is Sally Ride famous?
options: She was the first woman to play tennis
She was the first person to build a shuttle
She was the first girl to study science
She was the first American woman in space
questions.explanation: The article says that in 1983 she became the first American woman to travel to space. She loved tennis, but that is not why she is famous.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. Priya was "thankful" for the help with her science project. What does "thankful" mean?
questions.explanation: The suffix -ful means "full of," so thankful means full of thanks. Without thanks would be thankless.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. Ben "disagreed" with his friend about which team would win the game. What does "disagreed" mean?
questions.explanation: The prefix dis- means "not," so disagreed means did not agree. Ben and his friend picked different teams.

questions.stem: What does the cast list at the top of the play scene tell the reader?
options: What Dev says at the end
questions.explanation: A cast list names the characters before the scene begins. Where the cage is comes from the stage directions, not the cast list.

questions.stem: In "The Water Cycle," what happens right after water turns into a gas and rises?
options: It falls down as rain or snow
questions.explanation: The word Next shows that the gas cools and forms clouds after it rises. Rain and snow fall later, when the drops grow heavy.

questions.stem: The words "audience," "audio," and "audible" all share the Latin root "aud." What does "aud" mean?
questions.explanation: An audience listens to a show, and an audible sound is one you can hear. Port is the root that means to carry.

questions.stem: Why does Grace work so hard on her project?
options: She wants to be a scientist
Her teacher made her stay up
questions.explanation: Grace says she wants to be a scientist someday and that scientists check their work. Nothing in the story says she wants to beat Lily.

questions.stem: According to "Day and Night," what causes day and night on Earth?
options: The sun moving across the sky
questions.explanation: The article says Earth spins once about every 24 hours, so each side faces the sun and then turns away. It says the sun does not really move across the sky.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. The wind "whispered" through the tall pine trees. What does the author mean by this personification?
questions.explanation: A whisper is soft and quiet, so the wind blew softly. Wind cannot really tell a secret; the author gives it a human action.

questions.stem: How are Maya and Mira alike?
options: Both like to read in corners
questions.explanation: The story says both sisters love animals and help at the shelter. Telling jokes is true only of Maya, and reading in corners only of Mira.

questions.stem: What is the author's point of view about school gardens?
options: They take up too much space
Only big schools can have one
questions.explanation: The author begins with "I believe every school should have a garden" and gives reasons. The author says a garden does not need much space.

questions.stem: Read the sentence. Rosa put a "stamp" on the letter before she mailed it to her cousin. Which meaning of "stamp" is used in the sentence?
options: to bring a foot down hard
a loud stomp of the feet
questions.explanation: Before mailing a letter, you put a stamp on it to pay for postage. To stamp your foot is another meaning that does not fit here.

questions.stem: From whose point of view is "Biscuit Comes Home" told?
options: An older child in the family
questions.explanation: The narrator says I and talks about my little sister, Zoe. So the story is told by Zoe's older brother or sister, not by Zoe or the dog.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the best summary of the story?
options: A girl colors red hearts on twenty posters
A dog sleeps on a porch with a red collar
A family walks the block and calls a dog's name
A family uses posters to find their lost dog
questions.explanation: A summary tells the most important events: the dog gets lost, the family makes posters and he is found. The other choices are only small details from the story.

questions.stem: How does Zoe's crying change from the start of the story to the end?
questions.explanation: Zoe cries hard when Biscuit is lost, and at the end she cries happy tears. The order is from sad to happy, not the other way.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the last paragraph of the story?
options: To show how the narrator changed
To tell how Biscuit got out
To explain how to make a poster
questions.explanation: The last paragraph tells that the narrator now checks the gate and keeps a poster to help others, which shows what the narrator learned. It does not tell how Biscuit got out.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of "The Pony Express"?
options: Riders made mail faster until the telegraph
Riders crossed rivers and snowy mountains
Many people moved to California in the 1850s
Riders carried the mail in leather covers
questions.explanation: The article tells how the Pony Express made mail faster and why it ended when the telegraph came. Crossing rivers and mountains is a detail from one section.

questions.stem: How is the article "The Pony Express" mostly organized?
options: As a list of the riders' names
As a comparison of two routes
As steps for how to ride a horse
In time order, from start to end
questions.explanation: The article moves from the 1850s to 1860 to 1861, telling events in the order they happened. It does not compare two routes.

questions.stem: Why did the Pony Express close after only about eighteen months?
options: The riders got lost in storms
questions.explanation: The last section says a telegraph message took minutes, so the Pony Express was no longer needed. Storms were a danger, but they did not make it close.

questions.stem: Why does the author explain that riders could switch to a fresh horse at each station?
options: To show how the mail moved fast
To show that horses were cheap
To show where the riders slept
To show how big the stations were
questions.explanation: Fresh horses could keep galloping, which is why a letter could arrive in about ten days. The article never says the horses were cheap.

questions.stem: Read the sentences. Grace forgot her lines in the class play. Afterward her friend said, "It happens to everyone. Keep your chin up!" What does "keep your chin up" mean?
questions.explanation: Her friend wants Grace to stay hopeful and not feel sad. The idiom is not about where she points her chin.

questions.stem: Read the sentences. Owen wanted to rush through building his model bridge. His coach reminded him, "Slow and steady wins the race." What does the coach mean?
questions.explanation: The saying means that working carefully, step by step, leads to success. It is not really about running.

questions.stem: How does the setting change what Eli and his aunt do?
options: The cactus makes them turn back
questions.explanation: The desert is very hot, so they rest in the shade until it cools. The story has no rain, and the cactus plants do not make them turn back.

questions.stem: Which text structure does the author use in "A Cleaner Park"?
questions.explanation: The article tells about a problem, litter in the park, and how the students solved it with more cans and signs. That is a problem and solution structure.

questions.passage:
**Glossary**

**habitat**: the natural home of a plant or animal

**predator**: an animal that hunts other animals

**prey**: an animal that is hunted for food
questions.stem: Read the glossary and this sentence: The rabbit is "prey" for the fox. What does the sentence tell you about the rabbit?
questions.explanation: Prey is an animal that is hunted, so the fox hunts the rabbit. A predator is the one that does the hunting.

questions.stem: How does Chapter 3 fit into the whole story about Carlos?
options: It tells how he saved money
It tells about his school ride
It explains why he chose red
questions.explanation: Chapter 2 tells that Carlos kept falling, and Chapter 3 shows him finally riding on his own. Saving money happens in Chapter 1.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the idea that penguins are expert swimmers?
options: They are birds that cannot fly
Their wings are short and stiff
Penguins are a kind of bird
questions.explanation: Zooming forward by flapping their flippers shows how well penguins swim. That penguins cannot fly is true, but it does not show they swim well.

questions.stem: Read the sentences. When the team won the championship, the fans were not just happy. They were "___." Which word shows the strongest feeling?
